L884: ## Per-Platform Session Trackingcite79†​ L885: ### Gateway Sessionscite80†​ L886: 
L887: On messaging platforms, sessions are keyed by a deterministic session key built from the message source:
L888: Chat Type  | Default Key Format  | Behavior
L889: --- | --- | ---
L890: Telegram DM  | `agent:main:telegram:dm:<chat_id>`  | One session per DM chat
L891: Discord DM  | `agent:main:discord:dm:<chat_id>`  | One session per DM chat
L892: WhatsApp DM  | `agent:main:whatsapp:dm:<canonical_identifier>`  | One session per DM user (LID/phone aliases collapse to one identity when mapping exists)
L893: Group chat  | `agent:main:<platform>:group:<chat_id>:<user_id>`  | Per-user inside the group when the platform exposes a user ID
L894: Group thread/topic  | `agent:main:<platform>:group:<chat_id>:<thread_id>`  | Shared session for all thread participants (default). Per-user with `thread_sessions_per_user: true`.
L895: Channel  | `agent:main:<platform>:channel:<chat_id>:<user_id>`  | Per-user inside the channel when the platform exposes a user ID
L896: When Hermes cannot get a participant identifier for a shared chat, it falls back to one shared session for that room.
L897: ### Shared vs Isolated Group Sessionscite81†​ L898: 
L899: By default, Hermes uses `group_sessions_per_user: true` in `config.yaml`. That means:
L900: 
L901:   * Alice and Bob can both talk to Hermes in the same Discord channel without sharing transcript history
L902:   * one user's long tool-heavy task does not pollute another user's context window
L903:   * a running turn is keyed to the sender that started it, but `/stop` still reaches it — see below
L904: `/stop` means "stop what is running in this chat": it first tries the caller's own session key, then any live turn in this chat — other participants' runs in the caller's own thread included — authorization-gated, and never another room, workspace or profile. So an idle Alice's `/stop` can end a turn Bob (or a bot) started in the room she is in.
L905: A `/stop` sent from inside a thread is narrower: it reaches runs belonging to that thread and a room-wide run that carries no thread slot (the rolling-DM shape), but never another thread of the same channel and never a peer's per-sender top-level run.
L906: If you want one shared "room brain" instead, set:
L907: 
L908:     `
L909: 
L910:     group_sessions_per_user: false
L911: 
L912:     `
L913: 
L914: That reverts groups/channels to a single shared session per room, which preserves shared conversational context but also shares token costs, interrupt state, and context growth.
L915: ### Session continuitycite82†​ L916: Gateway conversations do not reset after inactivity or at a daily boundary. Use `/new` or `/reset` for an explicit new conversation; context compression remains automatic. Core ignores legacy `session_reset` settings, reset-policy overrides and reset-timer environment variables. If your config still sets `session_reset.mode` to `idle`, `daily` or `both`, gateway startup and `hermes doctor` warn about it.
L917: To keep time-based resets, install the catalog plugin that reads the same block unchanged: `hermes plugins install hermes-session-reset-policy`. Cached agents may be released to reclaim resources without replacing the durable conversation. Restart-recovery freshness limits automatic continuation, not the history loaded when you send a message.
L918: ### Session hygiene: why you should still run `/new`cite83†​ L919: 
L920: Because gateway conversations never expire on their own, it is easy to run one session for weeks. That works, but it quietly defeats the learning loop and inflates costs:
L921:   * Memory only pays off at boundaries. `MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` are injected at session start, and `session_search` exists to recall what fell out of context. In a never-ending session everything is still in context, so the agent has no reason to consult memory — the "self-learning" machinery barely runs. Memory distillation (the save before reset) also only happens when a session actually ends.
L922:   * Cost grows with history. Compression keeps a long session functional, but every turn still carries a large (compacted) prefix. A fresh session with distilled memory is almost always cheaper than a month-old thread.
L923: Practical rule: end a session when you finish a task or topic. Run `/new` (optionally named, e.g. `/new payments-refactor`) at natural stopping points — daily or per-project both work. Before the reset, ask the agent to "remember anything worth keeping" if the work surfaced durable preferences or procedures; it saves memories and skills from the expiring session automatically, but an explicit nudge helps. Restarting the machine or the gateway is not a boundary — the same session resumes.
L924: See cite84†Memory for what gets carried across boundaries.
L925: ### Continuity After Crashes and Restartscite85†​ L926: 
L927: A gateway chat is designed to be one continuous session — compacted repeatedly as it grows — until you explicitly run `/new` (or `/reset`). This holds across gateway crashes, restarts, and updates:
L928:   * Session identity (routing key, chat, origin) is written atomically when the session row is created, on every creation path (`/new`, first message, `/branch` children). If that write ever fails, the very next turn's routing refresh repairs the row automatically.
L929:   * After a restart, the gateway re-resolves each chat to the session with the most recent actual activity — an older, stale row can never win over the conversation you were actually having.
L930:   * Recovery respects `/new` boundaries: if the most recent event for a chat is an intentional reset, recovery starts fresh rather than reaching behind the reset to resurrect an older session. Elapsed time alone never prevents recovery of a durable conversation.
L931: ## Storage Locationscite86†​ L932: What  | Path  | Description
L933: --- | --- | ---
L934: SQLite database  | `~/.hermes/state.db`  | All session metadata + messages with FTS5
L935: Gateway messages  | `~/.hermes/state.db`  | SQLite — canonical store for all session messages
L936: Gateway routing index  | `gateway_routing` table in `~/.hermes/state.db`  | Maps session keys to active session IDs (origin metadata, expiry flags)
L937: Legacy routing mirror  | `~/.hermes/sessions/sessions.json`  | Backward-compat mirror of the routing index, written when `gateway.write_sessions_json: true` (the default)
L938: The SQLite database uses WAL mode for concurrent readers and a single writer, which suits the gateway's multi-platform architecture well.
L939: 
L940: `sessions.json` is not the session list
L941: The gateway routing index lives in the `gateway_routing` table inside `state.db`; `~/.hermes/sessions/sessions.json` is a legacy mirror of it, kept for backward compatibility (disable with `gateway.write_sessions_json: false`). It maps messaging session keys (`agent:main:<platform>:...`) to active session IDs. It only ever contains gateway/messaging entries, so if you run a messaging platform you'll see only those (e.g. `agent:main:whatsapp:dm:...`).
L942: This is expected and does not mean your CLI sessions are missing. `hermes sessions list`, `/sessions`, and the dashboard all read `state.db`, which holds every session (CLI, TUI, and gateway). The `/save` snapshots under `~/.hermes/sessions/saved/*.json` are convenience exports, not the index.
L943: If CLI sessions genuinely don't appear in `hermes sessions list`, the cause is `state.db` not receiving them — run `hermes sessions repair` and watch for a `⚠ Session store unavailable` warning at CLI startup, which means SQLite persistence failed for that run.
L944: 
L945: Legacy JSONL transcripts
L946: Sessions created before state.db became canonical may have leftover `*.jsonl` files in `~/.hermes/sessions/`. They are no longer written or read by Hermes. Safe to delete after verifying the corresponding session exists in state.db.
L947: ### Database Schemacite87†​ L948: 
L949: Key tables in `state.db`:
L950: 
L951:   * sessions — session metadata (id, source, user_id, model, title, timestamps, token counts). Titles have a unique index (NULL titles allowed, only non-NULL must be unique).
L952:   * messages — full message history (role, content, tool_calls, tool_name, token_count)
L953:   * messages_fts — FTS5 virtual table for full-text search across message content
L954: 
L955: ## Session Expiry and Cleanupcite88†​ L956: ### Automatic Cleanupcite89†​ L957:   * Gateway conversations persist across inactivity; use `/new` or `/reset` for an explicit boundary
L958:   * Before reset, the agent saves memories and skills from the expiring session
L959:   * Auto-pruning (on by default since #54189): when `sessions.auto_prune` is `true`, ended sessions inactive for `sessions.retention_days` (default 90) are pruned at CLI/gateway/cron startup
L960:   * `sessions.retention_days` must be a whole number of days `>= 0`. A negative value (or a missing one) is rejected: startup maintenance logs a warning naming the allowed range and skips the sweep instead of treating the future cutoff as "everything" — `sessions.auto_prune: false` is the switch that disables pruning
L961:   * After a prune that actually removed rows, `state.db` is `VACUUM`ed to reclaim disk space only when both gates pass: at least `sessions.min_vacuum_interval_days` (default 30) have elapsed since the last successful `VACUUM`, and more than 25% of the file's pages are reclaimable (`PRAGMA freelist_count / page_count`). A dense database never pays for a full rewrite to reclaim a few MB (SQLite does not shrink the file on plain DELETE)
L962:   * Pruning runs at most once per `sessions.min_interval_hours` (default 24); the last-run timestamp is tracked inside `state.db` itself so it's shared across every Hermes process in the same `HERMES_HOME`
L963: Without pruning, `state.db` grows without bound — multi-GB files within weeks were reported on gateway + cron installs. If you would rather keep every ended session forever (the pre-#54189 behavior), turn it off in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
L964: 
L965:     `
L966: 
L967:     sessions:
L968: 
L969:       auto_prune: false         # default is true — set false to keep all history
L970: 
L971:       retention_days: 90        # keep ended sessions active within this window
L972:       vacuum_after_prune: true  # reclaim disk space after a pruning sweep
L973: 
L974:       min_vacuum_interval_days: 30 # don't rewrite the DB more often than this
L975: 
L976:       min_interval_hours: 24    # don't re-run the sweep more often than this
L977: 
L978:     `
L979: Existing installs that already set any of these keys explicitly keep their values; only unset keys pick up the new defaults.
L980: Only ended sessions are ever deleted. Active sessions are never auto-pruned, regardless of age. Ended sessions are aged from their last activity — the freshest of live activity, latest message, or session start — so a long-lived conversation used recently is not deleted merely because it began before the retention window.
L981: The same holds for a conversation that compression split into several sessions: its older segments are kept while any later segment is, and are pruned together with it once the whole conversation qualifies.
L982: Stale open sessions from automation. Some producers — cron jobs, kanban workers, subagents, one-shot CLI runs — can die without ever marking their session ended, and pruning only deletes ended rows.
L983: To keep those from accumulating forever, each auto-prune pass also closes open sessions from those state-owned sources (`cli`, `cron`, `kanban`, `acp`, `api_server`, `subagent`, `tool`, plus the `recovered` placeholders that `hermes sessions recover` synthesizes for orphaned messages) whose last activity is older than `retention_days` (`end_reason: startup_orphan_reap`).
L984: Closing is non-destructive — the session stays resumable — and the row is aged from its close, so it is only deleted by a later pass after a further full retention window. Messaging platform sessions (Telegram, Discord, …), TUI/desktop sessions, pinned sessions, and sessions with a live turn or compression in progress are never closed by this sweep.
L985: ### Oversized-Transcript Guardscite90†​ L986: 
L987: Two limits stop a runaway transcript from being loaded into memory all at once (both default to `20000` active messages; `0` disables the guard):
L988: 
L989:     `
L990: 
L991:     sessions:
L992: 
L993:       max_resume_messages: 20000   # interactive resume (CLI / TUI / Desktop)
L994: 
L995:       max_export_messages: 20000   # one-shot in-memory export of a single session
L996: 
L997:     `
L998: 
L999: `max_resume_messages` bounds what the resume actually loads, not the whole history of the conversation:
L1000:   * A plain interactive resume (CLI `--resume`, the TUI) materializes the full compression lineage — every compacted segment plus the live tip — so it is bounded across the lineage.
L1001:   * Desktop's cold resume pages the transcript over REST and only holds the live tip segment in memory, so it is bounded by the tip alone. A long-lived chat that has been compacted many times (dozens of segments, tens of thousands of archived rows behind a small tip) is exactly what compression is meant to produce and opens normally; its footer message count reflects the stored lineage, not the live prompt.
L1002: When a resume is refused the client receives error code `4130` with the count and the scope it was measured against (`across its lineage` or `in its tip segment`). `hermes sessions export` still works for such sessions.
L1003: ### Manual Cleanupcite91†​ L1004: 
L1005:     `
L1006: 
L1007:     # Prune sessions older than 90 days
L1008: 
L1009:     hermes sessions prune
L1010: 
L1011:     # Delete a specific session
L1012: 
L1013:     hermes sessions delete <session_id>
L1014: 
L1015:     # Export before pruning (backup)
L1016: 
L1017:     hermes sessions export backup.jsonl
L1018: 
L1019:     hermes sessions prune --older-than 30 --yes
L1020: 
L1021:     `
L1022: 
L1023: tip
L1024: Auto-prune is on by default: ended sessions that have been inactive for `sessions.retention_days` (default 90) are removed at startup, and active sessions are never touched (see cite89†Automatic Cleanup above). Session history powers `session_search` recall across past conversations, so if you want to keep every ended session forever, set `sessions.auto_prune: false` in `config.yaml`, or raise `retention_days`.
L1025: With auto-prune off, `hermes sessions prune` remains available for one-off cleanup (observed failure mode without any pruning: a 384 MB `state.db` with ~1000 sessions slowing down FTS5 inserts and `/resume` listing).

L31: # Secure Env Ingress
L32: 
L33: Platform-independent, profile-scoped HTTPS forms for adding missing dotenv variables from Hermes messaging gateways. `/senv name KEY1,KEY2` defines a form; `/senv name` reopens it; `/senv status`, `/senv cancel`, and `/senv setup` provide readiness, invalidation and installation assistance. Never put values in chat. Form values travel browser → HTTPS → add-only target, not through the agent.
L34: This is the runtime-only catalog distribution, without privileged certificate installers. Python 3.11+, Linux/POSIX and trusted IP-address TLS material are required. Registration uses the normalized `pre_gateway_dispatch` hook plus the generic plugin slash command; no Telegram-specific handler is installed. Set `allowed_owners: {discord: ["exact-opaque-user-id"]}` for platform-specific owners, or keep legacy `allowed_telegram_user_ids: [123456789]` for Telegram.
L35: Chat allowlists alone do not grant ownership. Ordinary browser forms need no Telegram token; Telegram Mini App launch is unavailable through this generic command path.
L36: Bearer-link warning: the one-use HTTPS URL is returned to the originating chat. Anyone who reads the link can use it. Send `/senv` only in private or operator-trusted groups/threads, never in public or untrusted rooms. Never forward or log links. If the agent is busy, the host may queue, steer, interrupt or interpret the command; wait for completion or use `/stop` first, then send a fresh `/senv`. Do not assume busy commands avoid the model. A missing plugin cannot protect values already pasted into chat.
L37: `/senv setup` sends a fixed installation-only request using the host's existing injection permission, or supplies copyable ordinary-message text when injection is denied. Privileged changes need separate approval. No listener starts on import; TLS, target binding and owner authorization are checked before issuing a capability. Existing keys are never overwritten.
L38: See the cite6†full setup, security boundaries and test instructions†github.com . Administrative helpers are separately reviewed operator tools, not catalog contents. Never run privileged helpers from a runtime-user-writable checkout.

**The user is substantially right: Hermes already supplies much of the proposed yyot functionality.** We should not invent custom work to justify the project.

1. **Credentials and TOTP already exist.** Hermes documents encrypted profile-scoped storage, origin-bound password/card filling outside model context, automatic TOTP generation, one-time verification prompts, password-manager integration, and add/remove controls. Reuse these. The demonstrated secure-entry surfaces are CLI/TUI/Desktop; a complete reviewer-friendly Slack credential flow remains **unverified**, not proven absent. [Passwords & Logins](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/)

2. **Browser automation already exists.** Official support includes Browser Use Cloud and CLI, multiple browser backends, persistent browser profiles, and per-task sessions. No justification for rebuilding browser tools. [Browser Automation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/)

3. **Multi-profile hosting already does substantial isolation.** One gateway can scope secrets, sessions, memory, logs, terminal/browser configuration, and integrations per profile. Sender routing plus correctly configured ingress rules may suffice for separate reviewers without custom routing code. Unmatched senders fall back to the default profile unless explicitly constrained. Profiles do not establish different users’ authority *inside one shared profile*. [Multi-profile gateways](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes)

4. **Shared conversation and recovery already exist.** Hermes supports shared channel/thread sessions and durable history across gateway restarts. That deserves a deployed test, not a replacement implementation. [Sessions](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions)

The narrow checks are: secure first-time collection through deployed Slack; fresh-browser credential/session reuse; meaningful revocation including saved cookies and active work; task recovery without duplicating consequential actions; and successful completion across websites.

There is also a community HTTPS secret-entry plugin, but its catalog distinguishes general environment-secret forms from Telegram-only browser-login saving. Do not assume complete Slack coverage. [Secure Env Ingress](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/plugins/secure-env-ingress/)

**Recommendation:** configure and deploy upstream Hermes with the available browser integration, run the assignment’s acceptance flows, and implement only demonstrated gaps. If configuration passes everything, hosting, integration, and credible evidence may be the entire required contribution.

**The user is substantially right: Hermes already supplies much of the proposed yyot functionality.** We should not invent custom work to justify the project.

1. **Credentials and TOTP already exist.** Hermes documents encrypted profile-scoped storage, origin-bound password/card filling outside model context, automatic TOTP generation, one-time verification prompts, password-manager integration, and add/remove controls. No justification for rebuilding browser tools. [Browser Automation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/)

# yyot v1 scope and release criteria ## State This is the revised v1 scope. The repository currently contains Git/Entire scaffolding only; no yyot application, deployed reviewer experience, or acceptance evidence exists yet. This document specifies required behavior, not implemented capabilities. Optimize for general browser-task capability and strong per-user security. Hermes Agent is the selected agent harness. Reuse its built-in messaging gateway and suitable tool integrations. TypeScript remains the user's preference for yyot-owned service and integration code where appropriate; run Hermes in its upstream runtime rather than reimplementing it in TypeScript. Hosting, browser/file capability, persistent storage, and per-user security integration still require validation. Slack is the v1 user interface, using Hermes' built-in Slack adapter. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Reviewers use the deployed app in the demo Slack workspace through its invitation/entry link. Inference is owner-funded; reviewers need neither a checkout nor an OpenAI account. ## Architecture: shared team context and private personal execution One Slack app connects collaborative team conversations and isolated personal Hermes runtimes. The diagram describes logical responsibilities; the gateway and broker can be modules in the same trusted yyot service. Hosting and storage providers are not selected by this diagram. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["One yyot Slack app
Shared channels/threads and private DMs"] <--> Gateway["Trusted Slack gateway
Verify sender and conversation audience"] Gateway <-->|Shared conversation| Team["Team Hermes context
Partitioned by authorized channel/project audience"] Gateway <-->|Private DM routing| Broker["yyot authorization broker
Private dispatch and controlled publication"] Team -->|Request private work| Broker Broker -->|Owner-approved content and audience| Team Broker <-->|Sahan-authorized execution| Sahan["Sahan's isolated Hermes runtime
Private profile and durable data"] Broker <-->|Nishank-authorized execution| Nishank["Nishank's isolated Hermes runtime
Private profile and durable data"] ``` Collaborative team context is required in v1. Maintain two visibility domains: shared team context contains authorized channel/thread conversations, team decisions, shared goals/progress, and deliberately shared documents/results; personal context contains DMs, private memory, credentials, browser state, private files/artifacts, and private execution observations. Shared context must respect its actual workspace/channel/project audience; membership in a workspace does not reveal private-channel context. Collaborators can continue a shared discussion and plan without automatically sharing personal account access. The private boundary includes each user's full personal Hermes runtime and persistent personal data: DM transcripts/session databases, memory, learned skills derived from private work, private logs, credentials, browser state, working files, and private artifacts. Provision a separate runtime environment and private data volume per owner, backed by owner-scoped durable storage. The team conversation runtime gets only authorized shared context and has no direct access to personal homes, credentials, or browser sessions. Personal runtimes may read team context their owners are authorized to see. Never automatically copy personal transcripts, memory, screenshots, tool results, files, or learned skills into shared team memory. Private results use 1:1 Slack DMs until the owner approves the specific content and audience for sharing. Never expose platform/database/storage administrator credentials to model-generated code. Use one Slack bot with authenticated audience/sender routing, team Hermes context for designated shared channels/projects, and fresh personal profiles for private interactions. Keep the message sender, shared task/context audience, and private execution owner as separate application fields. A team request that needs personal accounts or files dispatches through an owner-authorized broker into that owner's private runtime. Another collaborator may contribute to the shared plan but cannot silently take over that execution, reuse its account authority, or approve on its owner's behalf. The team runtime receives safe status and owner-approved results rather than raw private observations. Keep bot credentials in the trusted receiving gateway rather than copying the bot token into personal runtimes. Admission must reject unprovisioned requesters instead of exposing a shared personal default. Hermes supports shared room/thread sessions and profile selection, but those settings do not implement per-request user authority or whole-runtime sandbox dispatch. Reuse the Slack adapter and routing primitives where they meet the boundary, and implement yyot-owned provisioning, private execution dispatch, access checks, and publication where necessary. Audit shared ingress logs, caches, queues, memory providers, and delivery-recovery stores: private personal payloads must not be retained in an unscoped shared store, while intentionally shared payloads retain their audience access controls. The trusted ingress necessarily handles messages in transit; Slack and configured model providers also process their respective message content. Pin and validate the Hermes version used. See [shared session settings](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions), [shared-bot profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), [profile routing non-goals](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals), and [whole-runtime Docker deployment](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker/). ### Context and storage ownership | Data | Owner or audience | Access rule | | --- | --- | --- | | Team conversations, decisions, task progress, and team memory | Authorized workspace/channel/project audience | Scope retrieval and persistence to that audience. A shared runtime must not mix conversations with different access boundaries. | | Personal DMs, memory, learned skills, execution observations, and logs | Individual user | Keep within the owner's personal runtime and durable private storage boundary; never load automatically into team context. | | Credentials, browser sessions, working files, and private artifacts | Individual user | Only the owner's authorized private execution may use them. Personal runtimes cannot access another owner's storage. | | Deliberately shared documents and approved result copies | Explicit destination audience | Share only the approved content. The source private file and account remain private; sharing a result grants no account authority. | | Routing, run, approval, and recovery records | Verified sender, execution owner, and conversation audience recorded separately | Trusted yyot code enforces these fields. Persist private payloads within their owner's boundary and shared payloads within their audience boundary. | Keep durable history, task recovery state, and retained artifacts independently of a running worker's scratch disk. A restart must restore the same owner/audience boundaries. The team runtime and each personal runtime receive only scoped storage access; platform administrator credentials remain in trusted infrastructure. The concrete storage provider and artifact layout remain open. ### Shared task to private work to shared result 1. **Collaborate in the team thread.** Sahan requests a report and Nishank adds requirements. Both contributions enter the authorized shared task context. 2. **Authorize the private part.** If the report needs Sahan's account or private files, the broker verifies his authorization for that work, requests it privately if needed, and binds the work to his runtime. It supplies only team context he is allowed to read. 3. **Execute under Sahan's authority.** His personal Hermes runtime performs the work. Nishank can contribute to the team plan, but cannot redirect, resume, or approve Sahan's private execution through a thread follow-up. A changed private operation requires authorization covering that change; consequential actions receive their own owner confirmation. 4. **Return private output to Sahan.** Results and raw observations remain in his private boundary. Deliver the private result or a protected artifact link through his DM; raw observations are not automatically sent to Slack. The team receives only status appropriate for its audience, without private account details. 5. **Publish the selected result.** Sahan approves the specific content and destination audience. The broker publishes that content and records it in the corresponding team context. Changed content or audience requires fresh approval; source files, credentials, and raw observations remain private. This flow lets a team coordinate work that each account owner authorizes and performs through their own agent. Delegating account authority to another collaborator remains outside v1. Hermes integration points, browser/file execution, secure handoff, deployment, and restart persistence still need implementation and validation. ## Now: required behavior 1. **Execute general tasks and collaborate.** Understand natural-language requests across unfamiliar websites using one general execution engine. Discover, download, inspect, transform, and upload files when the task requires them. In shared team conversations, collaborators can contribute to a common task and reuse authorized shared decisions/progress across turns and restarts. Site-specific product scripts do not constitute general-task support. 2. **Collect and reuse access securely.** Collect passwords, API keys, TOTP setup keys, card details when required, and browser login/OAuth access through secure input or handoff outside chat and model inputs. Persist encrypted credentials and browser-session state, reuse supported access across tasks and fresh browser runs, generate TOTP codes outside model inputs, and let the owner revoke access. Revocation stops affected active execution and invalidates saved access/session state. 3. **Enforce ownership outside the model.** Derive the message sender and audience from verified Slack identity and authorized conversation membership. Bind every private run, browser/session, credential lookup, file operation, private artifact, personal memory/learned skill, and private-history retrieval to its owner's isolated runtime/data boundary. Bind team history, memory, and shared artifacts to their authorized audience. Another participant's follow-up can contribute shared task context but conveys no authority over a collaborator's private execution or accounts. Keep model-generated code isolated from platform master keys and other users' resources. 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, give brief useful progress, clarify only material details, and provide private human login/verification handoff when necessary. Persist the goal and progress across access expiration or failures. Resume after the owner supplies what is needed, without blindly repeating completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain the owner's confirmation before a concrete consequential action such as a purchase, external message, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Verify the actual website state or intended artifact before declaring completion. Keep private account observations and results private until their owner approves specific content and its audience for sharing. Persist approved shared results with that audience scope; an approval to share a result does not grant account or filesystem access. These controls are application and execution-environment responsibilities. Hermes chat-session separation, profiles, allowlists, prompt instructions, separate browser profiles, or encrypted secret storage alone do not prove isolation or prevent observation leakage. Validate ownership across Hermes memory, session recall, learned skills, file/browser tools, and any enabled background jobs. Disable features whose data or authority cannot be scoped safely to their owner. Document and test the actual boundaries. ## Four deliverables | Deliverable | Completion criteria | | --- | --- | | Runnable repository | Dependency locks, setup instructions, environment-variable examples containing no secrets, and relevant verification instructions are included and exercised. | | Deployed reviewer experience | The backend and execution environment remain available without the developer's laptop. Two reviewers can enter through the Slack workspace invitation/entry link and use the app independently without local setup or an OpenAI account. | | Approximately two-minute yyoreel demo | A real request, secure access collection or handoff, and verified completion are shown. Include reuse/recovery where practical. Inspect the exported recording for exposed secrets before sharing it. | | Access-management and known-limits note | Explain verified identity/isolation, secret and browser-session storage, TOTP, reuse, revocation, observation leakage limits, and unsupported cases. Distinguish implemented and tested behavior from planned behavior. | ## Release evidence 1. Complete real tasks on at least two different websites through the same general engine, without preselected site-specific product flows; verify destination state rather than relying on the agent's completion message. 2. Find the intended requester-owned sandbox file and complete a browser upload. Also complete download, inspection/transformation, and upload as one task; verify the uploaded file is the intended artifact. 3. Collect access and a TOTP setup key through secure input, then demonstrate credential/TOTP reuse with a fresh browser run. Test session reuse separately, and verify revocation prevents subsequent reuse. 4. Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, provide the required owner input, and resume the persisted task successfully without replaying a completed consequential action. 5. Demonstrate two users contributing to the same shared task and reusing authorized team context after restart. Run adversarial checks: forged owner/account references, cross-user private file/artifact requests, another participant's thread follow-up, private-history/memory/learned-skill retrieval, and copied approval/handoff controls must not obtain another user's authority or private data. Verify concurrent private executions remain independent, a collaborator cannot approve an owner's action, and changed action details cannot reuse an earlier approval. Inspect transcripts, logs, memory-provider writes, and delivery/cache records for audience-scoped persistence. Demonstrate an owner-approved result becoming available to the team while its source private file, credentials, and raw observations remain protected; a shared turn must not automatically consume private state. Done means the required behavior is implemented, the four deliverables exist, and this evidence passes with honestly recorded limits. A video, a happy-path upload, or a deployed chatbot alone is not completion. If a required capability remains unsupported, report that gap explicitly rather than marking v1 complete. ## Later Additional interfaces beyond Slack, delegated use of another person's accounts, advanced cross-team memory/grants, and the configurable coding-agent-style approval-policy UX are deferred until after v1. Basic shared team conversation/task memory and explicit sharing of selected results are in v1. Hermes' built-in channel adapters can be evaluated when additional interfaces are needed. Ordinary owner confirmations remain in v1. ## Next Prove the execution path before broader implementation: one Slack app using Hermes' adapter, two users contributing to shared team context, owner-authorized dispatch into a full isolated personal Hermes runtime/data volume, file upload, durable team context and private history/artifacts across runtime restart, private login handoff, and explicit publication of an approved result back to the team. Validate conversation visibility, execution ownership, and publication separately rather than assuming shared sessions, profiles, or a terminal backend provide the boundaries. Then build the required behavior and collect the release evidence. Obtain the user's review before external submission or contacting the founders; this scope update authorizes neither.
